prompt: A checkout experiment picks a variant on every page load rather than once per visitor, so one person can bounce between the two designs inside a single session. What breaks first, and how does the readout mislead you?
criteria: Names the randomization unit as the thing chosen wrong
States that a visitor who sees both variants contaminates the contrast between them
Says the measured difference shrinks toward zero rather than growing
Names per-visitor assignment, held in a cookie or a user id, as the fix

prompt: A teammate plans to watch the experiment dashboard each morning and stop the test on the first day the p-value dips under 0.05. Write the pushback you would give them.
criteria: States that repeated looks push the false positive rate far above 5 percent
Explains that stopping on the first dip selects for random highs in the estimate
Names a sample size fixed in advance as one remedy
Names a sequential testing correction as the alternative to simply waiting it out

prompt: A discount test is randomized per customer, but the significance test is run over orders, and frequent buyers place dozens of orders each. What is the main flaw?
options: Nothing is wrong: more orders simply means more statistical power
Orders from the same customer are correlated, so the variance is understated and the p-value comes out too small
Orders cannot be counted until the test has run for a full purchase cycle
Randomizing per customer forces the two arms to end up different sizes

prompt: Which of these are settled before launch when an experiment is pre-registered?
options: The primary metric, and the exact query that computes it
The smallest effect worth detecting, and the sample size that follows from it
How many days the test runs, and what would justify an early stop
The multiplicity correction applied across the secondary metrics
Which subgroup to headline, picked once you can see where the lift landed
The significance threshold, moved to 0.10 after the result comes in at 0.08

prompt: A satisfaction survey goes to every customer, 8% of them answer, and the mean score is 4.6 out of 5. Explain which population that 4.6 actually describes, and which direction it is likely off.
criteria: Says the number describes respondents rather than the customer base
States that answering a survey is itself a choice tied to how someone feels
Commits to a direction and gives a reason, such as the most engaged or most angry over-responding
Names a check, such as comparing respondent traits against the full base or chasing a random subsample

prompt: A slide claims the funds on a platform returned 9% a year over the past decade, computed from the funds the platform lists today. Write what you would say to the person presenting it.
criteria: Points out that funds closed or merged during the decade are absent from the list
States that the funds which vanished are the ones that performed worst
Says the 9% figure overstates what an investor a decade ago would have earned
Names the fix, such as starting from the fund list as it stood ten years ago and following every fund forward

prompt: This query is meant to answer "how long does a new signup take to make a first purchase?". One line quietly changes which population the answer describes — which one?
lines: JOIN first_purchase p ON p.user_id = s.user_id
why: The inner join keeps only signups that eventually bought, so every signup still sitting at zero purchases drops out of the denominator. What comes back is the average wait among buyers — faster than the honest answer, and silent about the people the question is really about. A LEFT JOIN, with the never-buyers counted and reported as their own share, answers what was asked.

prompt: True or false: five design traits shared by every app that reached the top 100 downloads last year are evidence that those traits drive downloads.
criteria: Says the apps that had the same traits and failed were never in the sample
States that the rate of those traits among unsuccessful apps is unknown
Names a comparison group of non-survivors as what the claim needs
Notes that filtering on the outcome is what manufactures the apparent pattern

prompt: A result lands at a 2.1% lift with a 95% confidence interval running from -0.4% to 4.6%. Put that interval into a sentence a non-analyst would follow, without using the word significant.
criteria: Describes the interval as the range of true effects the data cannot rule out
Stops short of treating 2.1 percent as the effect that was established
States that zero sits inside the range, so no change at all stays plausible
Notes that more data narrows the range rather than pulling it toward the estimate

prompt: A product manager reads p = 0.31 and writes in the summary that the new flow has no effect on conversion. Draft the correction you would send back.
criteria: States that failing to detect an effect is not the same as showing there is none
Asks what effect size the test had the power to detect
Uses the confidence interval bounds to say what the data does rule out
Supplies replacement wording that leaves the uncertainty visible

prompt: What does the 95% in a 95% confidence interval actually refer to?
options: 95% of individual users fall inside the range
There is a 95% chance the true effect sits inside this particular interval
Across repeated samples, 95% of intervals built this way would contain the true effect
The finding would repeat in 95 of the next 100 experiments

prompt: Fill the blank: planning a test at 80% ______ means that even if the true effect is exactly the size you designed for, you would still miss it roughly one run in five.

A readout says conversion fell from 4.1% to 3.8% quarter over quarter and concludes the funnel is degrading. Elsewhere in the same data, mobile and desktop conversion each rose, and mobile went from 40% to 65% of traffic. Critique the conclusion, and say what the readout should have said.
criteria: Names the shift in traffic mix as the cause of the aggregate drop
States that both segments improved, which leaves the degrading-funnel claim unsupported
Explains the aggregate as a volume-weighted average of the segment rates
Rewrites the finding as growth inside each segment plus a move toward the weaker-converting channel

prompt: Every segment moves one way and the total moves the other. When is reporting the total still the right call, and when is it the wrong one?
criteria: Names a case where the aggregate is the quantity actually paid or felt, such as total revenue or total support cost
States that the mix shift can itself be the result worth managing rather than noise to strip out
Says the size of the mix change has to travel alongside the aggregate either way
Names a case where mix-adjusting would bury a real decline, such as a deliberate push into a weaker channel

prompt: A page test, split by device. Desktop: variant B converts 50 of 100, variant A converts 180 of 400. Mobile: variant B converts 40 of 400, variant A converts 5 of 100. B therefore wins on both devices. Pooling the two devices together, what is B's overall conversion rate?
explain: B pools to (50 + 40) / (100 + 400) = 90/500 = 18%. A pools to (180 + 5) / (400 + 100) = 185/500 = 37%. B wins desktop (50% vs 45%) and mobile (10% vs 5%) and still loses the pooled comparison by nineteen points, because four fifths of B's traffic is mobile — where almost nobody converts — while four fifths of A's is desktop. The pooled figures are weighted averages, and here the weights, not the conversion rates, pick the winner.

prompt: An aggregate metric moved and you suspect the segment mix rather than the metric itself. Put these five steps in the order you would do them.
items: Recompute the aggregate with the earlier period's segment shares held fixed
Confirm the aggregate move is real and not a date-range or pipeline artifact
Report the per-segment direction together with the size of the mix change
Split the metric by the suspected segment and check the direction inside each
Compare each segment's share of total volume across the two periods

prompt: On a machine with a single core, a program appears to handle four downloads at once. Explain how that happens when no two instructions ever execute at the same instant, and what it does to total CPU time.
criteria: Describes the tasks taking turns, switching when one waits or is preempted
States that concurrency is interleaving while parallelism needs more than one core
Says the interleaving does not reduce the total CPU work
Explains the speedup as filling time that was otherwise spent waiting on the network

prompt: Match each workload or description on the left to the execution model on the right that fits it.
left: Fetching 500 URLs, where nearly all the time is spent waiting on the network
Re-encoding 5,000 video thumbnails on an eight-core box
Two instructions executing during the very same clock cycle
Four tasks each making progress by taking turns on one core
right: Parallelism, which requires more than one core
A thread pool, or async I/O on a single thread
Concurrency, which requires only a scheduler
A process pool with one worker per core

prompt: True or false: a program written to be concurrent will run faster once you move it onto a machine with more cores.
criteria: Separates concurrency as a way of structuring work from parallelism as simultaneous execution
Names a workload that gains nothing, such as one serialized behind a single lock or blocked on network waits
States that a speedup needs work that is both splittable and CPU-bound
Mentions the serial fraction or the coordination overhead capping what extra cores can buy

prompt: Two requests each read a counter showing 41, each add one, and each write 42, so one increment vanishes. Walk through the interleaving, then explain why adding a short sleep or a retry does not fix it.
criteria: Lays out the order as read, read, write, write across the two requests
States that the read-modify-write is three separate steps with nothing holding them together
Says a sleep only narrows the window and leaves it open
Names a fix that makes the update atomic, such as UPDATE SET n = n + 1, one mutex around all three steps, or a compare-and-swap loop

prompt: A bug report says stock levels occasionally go negative. The fix up for review wraps the existing check-then-decrement in a try block that retries three times on failure. Critique it.
criteria: States that a retry does nothing to stop two writers from both passing the check
Identifies check-then-act, with a gap between the check and the write, as the race
Names an atomic replacement, such as one conditional UPDATE carrying a quantity guard, a row lock, or a database constraint
Points out that the retry re-runs the same unsafe sequence and can mask the failure

prompt: This helper is supposed to be callable from many threads, and the lock it uses is real. One line still loses increments — which one?
why: The write sits outside the `with lock` block, so the lock protects only the read. Two threads can each take the lock in turn, both read 41, both release, and then both assign 42 — one increment gone. The entire read-modify-write has to happen under the lock, which here means indenting the assignment so it lives inside the `with`.

prompt: Many threads increment one shared integer and the final count comes out low. Which of these changes actually make the increment safe?
options: Hold a single mutex across the read, the add, and the write
Have each thread sleep a random few milliseconds before writing
Replace the three steps with one atomic statement, such as a database UPDATE that sets n = n + 1
Give each thread a private counter and sum them once every thread has joined
Re-read the shared value immediately before writing, so the value used is fresh
Move the increment into a longer function so it runs start to finish in one go
